title: Difference-Aware Retrieval Policies for Imitation Learning
claim: Standard imitation discards its data at inference and maps the query directly to an action; ours retrieves neighbors and reasons over their differences.
layout: 2 panels split by dashed divider, left-to-right, dashed arrows from database to modules
description: Two panels separated by a vertical dashed gray line. The left panel, titled 'Imitation Learning', shows a blue cylinder database holding a 2x2 grid of robot-arm images, each labeled with a state s*_i and an action a*_i chip. Beside it, an orange rounded box holds the query state s_q with a green border and the policy f_theta. A solid arrow points down to the predicted action a-hat_q. The right panel, titled 'Difference-Aware Retrieval Policies', shows the same database. Dashed arrows run from individual entries to three stacked orange boxes, each with the neighbor state, its action, and the difference between the neighbor state and s_q, passed into f_theta, with ellipsis dots between them. An arrow leads down to a pink box with the actions a'_1 to a'_k aggregated by g_psi, then to a-hat_q.
caption: Overview of \ours: Unlike standard BC (left), \ours (right) utilizes a retrieval-based reparameterization centered around difference vectors between query states and retrieved neighbors. In standard behavior cloning, the dataset of expert state-action pairs is used only for training and is discarded at inference-time, while \ours utilizes it to perform retrieval to find a local neighborhood of expert state-action pairs around each query point $s_q$.
abstract: Parametric imitation learning via behavior cloning can suffer from poor generalization to out-of-distribution states due to compounding errors during deployment. We show that reusing the training data during inference via a semi-parametric retrieval-based imitation learning approach can alleviate this challenge. We present Difference-Aware Retrieval Policies for Imitation Learning (DARP), a semi-parametric retrieval-based imitation learning approach that addresses this limitation by reparameterizing the imitation learning problem in terms of local neighborhood structure rather than direct state-to-action mappings. Instead of learning a global policy, DARP trains a model to predict actions based on $k$-nearest neighbors from expert demonstrations, their corresponding actions, and the relative distance vectors between neighbor states and query states. DARP requires no additional assumptions beyond those made for standard behavior cloning -- it does not require additional data collection, online expert feedback, or task-specific knowledge. We demonstrate consistent performance improvements of 15-46% over standard behavior cloning across diverse domains, including continuous control and robotic manipulation, and across different representations, including high-dimensional visual features. Code and demos are available at https://weirdlabuw.github.io/darp-site/.
